questions.stem: Chris, 23, is ready to go home from the ED after successful needle aspiration of a left primary spontaneous pneumothorax. While you are giving safety-netting advice, he says he has booked a scuba diving course in Bali in three months. What is the most appropriate advice to give him?
options: He can dive once a repeat chest X-ray shows the lung has fully re-expanded
He should avoid diving for life unless he has definitive surgery to prevent recurrence
He can dive after 6 weeks if he has stopped smoking and has no symptoms
He can dive if he stays shallower than 10 m and ascends slowly on every dive
questions.why: Diving after a pneumothorax is avoided for life unless definitive surgery (such as VATS pleurectomy) has been done. Pressure changes on ascent can expand any trapped air into a tension pneumothorax underwater.
notes: Waiting for X-ray resolution is the rule for flying. It does not make diving safe, because the risk of recurrence stays high.
Stopping smoking lowers his recurrence risk, but not enough to make diving safe without definitive surgery.
Gas expands most in the shallowest 10 m, so a depth limit and slow ascents do not remove the risk of a pneumothorax.

questions.stem: Chris, 23, has a first left primary spontaneous pneumothorax measuring 3 cm at the hilum on an erect X-ray. He is breathless at rest, RR 26, SpO2 93% on room air, HR 110, BP 124/76, trachea central. He has no lung disease. What is the most appropriate next step in the emergency department?
options: Observe on high-flow oxygen and repeat the chest X-ray in 4 hours
Immediate needle decompression in the 2nd intercostal space
Needle aspiration with a 16–18 G cannula, then a repeat chest X-ray
Insert a large-bore (28 Fr) chest drain by blunt dissection
questions.why: A symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax needs intervention. First line is needle aspiration (or an ambulatory device), stopping once more than 2.5 L has been aspirated, followed by a repeat X-ray. If it fails, insert a small-bore drain.
notes: Conservative management suits patients with few symptoms; Chris is breathless at rest and hypoxic, so he needs the air removed.
Needle decompression is for tension, which is a clinical diagnosis; his BP is normal, the trachea is central and there is no mediastinal shift.
Large-bore drains are not first line for a primary spontaneous pneumothorax; if aspiration fails, a small-bore drain to an underwater seal is used.

questions.stem: Chris, 23, has a large left primary spontaneous pneumothorax with the left lung partly collapsed towards the hilum. His SpO2 is 93% on room air and he is breathing at 26/min. What is the main mechanism of his hypoxaemia?
options: Blood still perfusing the collapsed, poorly ventilated left lung (shunt)
Impaired diffusion across a thickened alveolar–capillary membrane
Global alveolar hypoventilation from splinting due to pleuritic pain
Increased dead space from ventilated lung that is no longer perfused
questions.why: Collapsed lung is still perfused but barely ventilated, so a low V/Q and shunt send deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts some of this blood away, which is why hypoxaemia is often only mild.
notes: Diffusion impairment is seen in interstitial lung disease or oedema; his alveolar membrane is normal.
Global hypoventilation would raise the PaCO2; he is tachypnoeic, and the problem lies in one lung, not in total ventilation.
Ventilated but unperfused lung (high V/Q, dead space) is the pattern of pulmonary embolism, not of a collapsed lung.

questions.stem: Chris's needle aspiration fails, and a small-bore chest drain is inserted in the left triangle of safety, 5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line. The clinician enters the space just above the upper border of the lower rib. Which anatomical fact explains this technique?
options: Internal thoracic artery runs along the upper border of each rib
Long thoracic nerve runs deep within each intercostal space
Main intercostal vessels run mid-space between adjacent ribs
Intercostal vein, artery and nerve lie in the groove under the rib above
questions.why: The main intercostal neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve, from top to bottom) runs in the costal groove along the lower border of each rib. Going in just above the rib below avoids it.
notes: The internal thoracic artery runs vertically about 1 cm lateral to the sternal edge; it matters for anterior approaches, not along each rib.
The long thoracic nerve runs on the surface of serratus anterior in the mid-axillary line, not inside the intercostal spaces.
The main bundle sits in the costal groove under the rib above, not mid-space; only small collateral branches run lower in the space.
